extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history / American Revolutionary history; readers interested in the development of early American newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of practices, standards, and constraints shaping American newspapers during the Revolutionary period (c.1765–1783) and the immediate Federalist era—covering content choices, production, distribution, partisanship, and commercial models. Useful for understanding how early newspapers were produced and evaluated in their historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndicated column / 'Journal of Occurrences'
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Journal of Occurrences' was edited by Boston Patriots for distribution throughout the colonies and in England and constitutes the first syndicated 'column' in American journalism; its purpose was propagandic but it was definitely a news feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a recurring syndicated column allowed a propagandistic, shareable day-by-day news budget; example: weekly Boston items copied by New York Journal and Pennsylvania Chronicle. Note that such columns mixed news with editorial purpose and could be reproduced widely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of news ('news as it drifted in')
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers generally 'took their news as it drifted in' and could not rely on prompt supply even from nearby papers, leading to widely varying publication dates for the same event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate newspapers by how promptly they reported events; examples show delays (Boston 'massacre' story a week later; Lexington/Battle reports appearing in different towns days or weeks apart). Timeliness was constrained by postal and wartime disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extras and advancing publication dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasional news enterprise: papers united to issue broadsides or 'extras' (e.g., repeal of the Stamp Act) or advanced their day of publication to get news to subscribers earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issuing extras or advancing schedules was a recognized tactic to break important news; absence of this tactic could be a negative in competitive timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and prevalence of rumors under wartime conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: War conditions and irregular arrival of English papers made rumors and false news more prevalent than under ordinary conditions (example: month-old reports anticipating war declarations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess reportage with awareness of source lag; verify cross-checking practices and note likelihood of rumor propagation when communication lines were poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution networks and postal reliability ('parliamentary post' / 'constitutional post')
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'parliamentary post' was given up in 1775 and the 'constitutional post' was inadequate; military operations and bad roads impeded postriders, stimulating private postrider systems and other workarounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution reliability is a key criterion: which postal system was used, whether private postriders or advertised letter-carriers were employed, and how the paper navigated wartime blockades affected reach and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local focus due to communication limits
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of proper communication, newspapers had perforce to remain local journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate geographic scope: many papers primarily served local communities; national reach was limited by communication constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content breadth (political/military vs other news)
rubrics_metrics.description: While the dominant running stories were taxes and the Revolution, papers also commonly printed accidents, wrecks, fires, storms, agricultural yields, 'remarkables' and monstrosities, gaol breaks, epidemics, medical achievements, and crime news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced newspaper of the period typically mixed political/military reporting with local and miscellany items; heavy concentration solely on one category (unless partisan mission) is notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary and marriage notice conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deaths and marriages were noted only for prominent persons and used conventional, sometimes quaint, phrasing; examples show very formal or flowery notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess notices for formality and social norms; departure toward more informal notices (as in some papers) indicates stylistic differences among publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline and typographic usage ('big-type headings')
rubrics_metrics.description: Big-type headings occasionally appeared over important news (one large line over the Declaration of Independence example), but these were seldom more than label headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the use of display typography: rare but significant headlines signaled importance; scarcity of display typography reflected material or stylistic limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead style: editorial comment vs factual lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads of important stories commonly consisted of editorial comment without factual details (e.g., Boston Gazette's lead on the 'massacre' was largely editorial before providing a 'circumstantial account').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether articles begin with factual journalism or with commentary—editorialized leads were common and point toward the nascent editorial form rather than neutral reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of news and editorial/commentary (forerunner of editorial column)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers showed recognition of distinction by printing comment in italics (Journal of Occurrences) or by placing editorials under the local heading; this practice pointed toward the editorial column as a separate form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate layout and typographic cues (italics, placement) used to demarcate opinion from news; clearer separation is an emerging professional practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion dissemination methods (letters and pen-names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion was still expressed mainly by letters signed by pen-names; editors were often printers/publishers, not primary authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how opinion appears—via editorials, signed/anonymous letters, or official resolutions. Heavy reliance on pen-name letters indicates a participatory/opinionated public sphere rather than formal editorial authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press freedom constraints: legal vs extra-legal pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal prosecutions were limited by grand juries' unwillingness to indict printers; however, mobs and threats of violence (especially from Sons of Liberty) exerted strong extra-legal pressure suppressing Tory or impartial papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the operating risks and environment: legal vulnerability was often low, but physical mob pressure could meaningfully curtail publishing and influence content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising patronage and content of ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising patronage maintained a high level during the war; ads included recruiting, solicitations for gifts (clothing for army), and a wider variety of goods and services; ad rates rose during the war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure a paper's commercial viability by ad volume and types. Ads served civic and military functions (e.g., recruiting), and ad design (borders, stock-cuts) varied with material shortages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper shortages and production constraints (stock-cuts, display typography)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shortage of paper sometimes caused omission of advertisements and decreased the use of stock-cuts and display typography; some papers used borders on ads as an innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production constraints directly affected visual richness and ad capacity; evaluate aesthetic and content truncation due to shortages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation size and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulations increased before the war; papers made claims (e.g., Rivington's 3,600; Isaiah Thomas 3,500; Connecticut Courant said to reach 8,000 in 1778), but many had only a few hundred subscribers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both claimed circulation and realistic readership (pass-along usage in homes, taverns); circulation influenced prestige and political influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription pricing and delinquency
rubrics_metrics.description: Subscription rates varied (from 6s8d to 26s); delinquents were a major problem affecting newspaper viability (printers sometimes lacked funds to buy paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economic health by subscription model, rates, and collection enforcement; unpaid subscribers could force size reductions or threaten survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution and last-mile delivery (private postriders, hawkers, apprentices)
rubrics_metrics.description: Private postriders carried competing papers between towns and collected subscription fees; within towns delivery shifted from printer's apprentices to independent men and lads; street hawkers sold papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess distribution methods for reach and business model: use of private postriders and hawkers increased circulation beyond formal postal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the postal reform and political control of mail
rubrics_metrics.description: Franklin's dismissal as Deputy Postmaster General and William Goddard's push for a 'Constitutional' postal system show postal organization was politically significant; the Continental Congress took over the American postal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how postal organization and political control of mail shaped access to news and fairness to partisan papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magazine viability and short-lived monthlies
rubrics_metrics.description: Only five monthly magazines were published in this period and they were brief experiments (three to nineteen months); noteworthy examples include the Pennsylvania Magazine and Brackenridge's United States Magazine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess magazine ventures for longevity and distinctive features (e.g., Paul Revere engravings); short runs indicate limited market or wartime constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth of press prestige and political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: By the end of the war journalism had made a distinct gain in prestige—credited with helping repeal the Stamp Act—and became a powerful arm of the Patriot movement; leaders like Washington actively encouraged and aided the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a paper's influence by its political alliances, endorsements, and recognition by leaders; institutional support (e.g., Washington sending tenting to papermills) signaled importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan founding and emergence of the editor as spokesman
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Revolution many papers were founded as spokesmen of political parties (Federalist vs Republican), giving a new dignity and personality to the editor who became more of a public figure rather than a mere printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial voice and founding purpose—papers explicitly created as party organs are to be read as partisan advocacy rather than neutral reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on shipping intelligence and commercial news
rubrics_metrics.description: Shipping intelligence and commercial news received careful attention, especially in port cities; this commercial content supported the emergence of advertising-heavy daily newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In mercantile centers, measure a paper's value by the quality and timeliness of shipping and commercial intelligence it provided; strong commercial pages supported daily formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication frequency and the economics of daily papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The move to daily publication required sufficient advertising patronage and operational capacity; early daily experiments (Ben Towne's Pennsylvania Evening Post; Pennsylvania Packet) show daily success depended on ad revenue and market size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate when and why papers transitioned to daily frequency: look for sufficient advertising, distribution networks, and urban readership to sustain daily issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of broadsides and collective publication for major events
rubrics_metrics.description: On major developments such as the repeal of the Stamp Act, Boston papers united to issue a broadside extra; broadsides or combined efforts provided immediate mass dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess responsiveness and collaboration among papers in extraordinary events; use of broadsides was an effective high-visibility tactic for important news.
